kurz: How the equity portion can be spread across the world's markets by market capitalisation or GDP, what role emerging markets and small caps play, and what overweighting the home market costs.

bloecke.md:
A world portfolio determines how the risky part of your wealth is spread across the world's equity markets. How large this part is has been decided beforehand and is not the topic here.

The usual approach is [[Market capitalisation weighting|market capitalisation weighting]]. Each company enters the index with the market value of its freely tradable shares, the [[Free float|free float]]. Holdings of the state and of anchor shareholders as well as locked-up blocks do not count, because they cannot be bought. Market weighting is the only weighting scheme that all investors can hold at the same time, because all portfolios together make up the market. If one investor deviates from market weighting, another must necessarily hold the opposite position. Every deviation is therefore an active bet, even if it is implemented with an index fund.

Market weighting is also low-maintenance and inexpensive. If a company's share price rises, its weight in the index rises by itself, without any shares having to be bought. This is why the ongoing charges of broad world ETFs are between 0.05% and 0.20% a year. Any different construction, by contrast, generates turnover and is more expensive.

The downside of this convenience is concentration. With market weighting, the most highly valued country, the most highly valued sector and the most expensive share automatically receive the greatest weight. The following chart shows the country weights in the MSCI World, the index of 23 developed markets, as of the end of August 2026.

bloecke.titel: Country weights in the MSCI World on 31 Aug 2026
bloecke.unter: The index covers 23 countries, but almost three-quarters of the index weight is accounted for by a single one of them, the USA. The ten largest individual constituents together made up 26.6%.

bloecke.md:
## Weighting by market value or GDP

[[GDP weighting]] is based on economic output instead of market value. Its advocates argue that market capitalisation only measures how much corporate value is listed on a capital market and how highly it is currently valued, but not how much is produced there. Countries with many unlisted family businesses are therefore underweighted, and countries with high valuations overweighted. Because gross domestic product does not depend on share prices, a GDP component also has a countercyclical effect. If the prices in a market rise sharply, its target weight falls in relative terms, and at the next rebalancing, shares there are sold.

The counterarguments carry just as much weight. GDP cannot be bought; what is bought is still shares, only in different proportions. The capital asset pricing model derives a premium for the market portfolio, but there is no comparable equilibrium theory for a GDP premium. Implementation costs turnover and bid-ask spread, and in Germany also taxes on realised gains. Over the past fifteen years, GDP weighting would moreover have cost return, because the highly valued US market kept rising.

GDP weighting can therefore be justified on grounds of diversification and valuation, but it does not promise a higher return. Investors who choose it reduce concentration on a single market and pay for this with costs and the risk of deviating from the market.

## Differences between world indices

The term “world ETF” is not protected. Funds on four index families that cover different things are all given this name. The MSCI World contains only developed markets, the MSCI ACWI and FTSE All-World also include emerging markets, and the ACWI IMI additionally includes small companies. FTSE classifies South Korea as a developed market, MSCI as an emerging market. For this reason alone, the percentages of two providers are never exactly comparable.

bloecke.titel: Four types of world index (products only as examples, not a recommendation)
US share by index type, reference dates July/August 2026
bloecke.unter: The asset class is the same in all four cases, but the weight of the USA differs widely. The range from 46% to 72% results solely from the construction rules.

bloecke.md:
## Emerging markets and the 70/30 split

By market capitalisation, emerging markets make up around 10 to 12% of the world equity market, by economic output a multiple of that. This difference gave rise to the best-known rule of thumb among German ETF investors. It provides for 70% MSCI World and 30% MSCI Emerging Markets, reset to the target allocation once a year. The rule is a rough approximation of GDP weighting with two building blocks.

How well it has performed depends entirely on the starting point. The following calculation uses the calendar-year returns of the MSCI indices in euros after withholding tax (Net Total Return) and the DAX performance index. Fund costs, trading costs and flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) are not taken into account.

bloecke.titel: Growth of €10,000, end of 2000 to end of 2025
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation from historical annual returns (MSCI net, EUR; DAX performance index). 70/30 with annual rebalancing, excluding costs and taxes.

bloecke.titel: The same data split into two periods (% p.a., euros, net)
Where the excess return came from
bloecke.md: Over 25 years, 70/30 at 6.90% a year was ahead of the pure developed-market index at 6.26%. The entire lead arose between 2001 and 2010. Since 2011, adding emerging markets has cost around 1.9 percentage points a year. Investors who deviate from market weighting must be able to hold out through decades in which this decision looks wrong. Otherwise they bail out at the worst possible moment.

bloecke.titel: Return difference, emerging minus developed markets, per calendar year (percentage points, EUR)
bloecke.unter: In the first ten years, emerging markets built up a lead; in the following fifteen years they were mostly behind. Whether a different regional weighting pays off only becomes clear over decades.

bloecke.md:
## Small caps in the world portfolio

An [[IMI]] index adds the small listed companies. When switching from the ACWI to the ACWI IMI, the number of constituents in the index more than triples, but the weights shift by only a few percentage points. Small companies are numerous, but their total market value is small. As a contribution to diversification, this extension is well founded and practically free of cost, because it represents the investable market more completely.

A deliberate overweighting of small caps, on the other hand, is a factor bet and no longer represents the market. Kenneth French's US data series shows around 1.4% a year for the size factor from 1926 to 2026, which is not statistically significant (t = 1.82). Since 1994 the figure has been minus 0.29% a year. Details and counterarguments follow in the lesson on factors.

Germany has a weight of less than 2.4% in the MSCI World and is not among the five largest countries in the index. A portfolio that is 30% invested in a DAX ETF therefore bets around thirteen times the world weight on a single country. From 2001 to 2025, the DAX returned 5.49% a year and the MSCI World 6.26%. In the years 2000 to 2002, the DAX lost around 58%, the MSCI World in euros around 45%. [[Home bias]] therefore does not cost return with certainty. It does, however, widen the dispersion of possible outcomes without this additional risk being rewarded.

A second, often overlooked part of the calculation lies outside the portfolio. Your job, salary, statutory pension entitlements, an owner-occupied property and usually also your bank balances already depend on the German economy and the German legal system. An additional overweighting of German shares increases concentration where the cluster risk lies anyway. The obvious justification that you know these companies better is almost always based on familiarity and not on better information. Familiarity provides no edge over the analysts who follow the same market.

## One ETF or several

The solution with a single broad fund has three advantages that apply regardless of convenience. First, rebalancing between regions takes place within the fund and therefore does not trigger any flat-rate withholding tax. Investors who reweight two ETFs by hand, by contrast, realise gains and, owing to the partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) of 30%, pay an effective 18.46% on them, plus church tax where applicable. Second, there is no weighting discipline that could be lost. Third, such funds are now cheaper than the sum of their building blocks. A broad all-country ETF costs from 0.07% a year.

The disadvantage is that you cannot control the regional allocation yourself, and a sale always sells all regions at the same time. For investors who want to set the allocation themselves or to make targeted withdrawals from one building block in the withdrawal phase, two or three positions offer more flexibility. For tax purposes, all the equity ETFs mentioned are treated the same. With an equity share permanently above 50%, a partial exemption of 30% applies, and for mixed funds with an equity share of 25% or more, only 15%.

## Kommer's approach and its critics

Gerd Kommer's world portfolio first separates the structure from the product. The structure consists of a risky portion of globally diversified shares and a low-risk portion of short-dated bonds of the highest credit quality or instant-access savings. The ratio of the two portions depends on risk-bearing capacity. Only after that is implementation decided. Its most consistent form is the ETF launched in 2023 on the Solactive Gerd Kommer Multifactor Equity Index.

This index differs from a market-weighted index in two rules. The country weighting is derived half from free-float market capitalisation and half from nominal GDP in dollars, and is capped at no more than twice and no less than half the pure market weight. Furthermore, no company may weigh more than 1% on the rebalancing date. As a result, the US share is 46.4% instead of just over 60% in the market-weighted ACWI IMI, and the ten largest positions together account for 9.5% instead of just under 22%. In addition, there are overweightings according to five factors and exclusions based on sustainability criteria.

The critics argue on the basis of costs and benefits. The fund costs 0.45% a year, an ACWI IMI ETF 0.17%. The correlation between the two is 0.97, and over 93% of the performance of the Kommer fund can be explained by the cheaper competitor alone. A factor regression over the short live history found a significant value only for the market factor. The index return of 10.06% a year since 31 July 2017 is moreover mostly back-calculated; the index has only been calculated live since May 2023.

€100,000 is invested for 30 years, with an assumed net return after fund costs.

- At 6.50% a year, the result is €661,400.
- At 6.22% a year, that is, 0.28 percentage points less, the result is €611,200.

The difference is around €50,200, or 7.6% of final wealth. A different construction must first make up this shortfall through additional return before it pays off. Taxes and the risk that the deviation goes in the wrong direction are not yet taken into account.

bloecke.md: First the equity allocation is set, then the coverage of world markets, and only last the fine-tuning. Investors who deviate from market weighting should be able to write down the reason in one sentence, as well as the sign by which they would recognise a mistake. If that is not possible, a broad, low-cost all-country index is the better choice. It is not necessarily optimal, but it requires no conviction that could be lost during ten years of weak results.

mitnehmen: Only market capitalisation weighting can be held by all investors at the same time, and every deviation from it is an active bet with a counterparty.
The term “world ETF” is not protected; the MSCI World covers only 23 developed markets, ACWI and All-World add emerging markets, and IMI additionally adds small caps.
The 70/30 split was ahead from 2001 to 2025 (6.90% versus 6.26% a year), but achieved its lead entirely before 2011 and has cost around 1.9 percentage points a year since then.

Germany weighs less than 2.4% in the MSCI World; home bias widens the dispersion of outcomes without being rewarded for it, and concentrates risk in the same place on which your job and pension already depend.

Constructions with a GDP component spread country risk visibly more widely, but must first make up for their extra cost through additional return, because 0.28 percentage points a year corresponds to around 7.6% of final wealth over 30 years.

begriffe.text: Weighting by the market value of the freely tradable shares. It is the only weighting that all investors can hold at the same time, and it is therefore the reference point against which every deviation is an active bet.
The freely tradable portion of a company's shares. State holdings and blocks held by families and anchor shareholders are not included, because they are not available to the market.

Country weighting by economic output instead of market value. It has a countercyclical effect and reduces concentration in highly valued markets. There is no theoretical justification for higher returns, and implementation generates turnover and costs.

The tendency to buy shares of the home market far beyond its world weight. Germany weighs less than 2.4% in the MSCI World. The overweighting widens the dispersion of outcomes without this being additionally rewarded.
Abbreviation for Investable Market Index. This index variant contains small listed companies in addition to large and mid-sized ones, and thus represents the investable market almost completely.
